In [[mathematics]], a [[ideal_(ring_theory)#Examples_and_properties|proper]] [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] of a [[commutative ring]] is said to be '''irreducible''' if it cannot be written as the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of two strictly larger ideals.<ref name="m98">{{citation|title=Algebraic Geometry|volume=136|series=Translations of mathematical monographs|first=Masayoshi|last=Miyanishi|publisher=American Mathematical Society|year=1998|isbn=9780821887707|page=13|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1reGWSo8XIsC&pg=PA13}}.</ref> 

==Examples==
* Every [[prime ideal]] is irreducible.<ref>{{citation|title=Advanced Algebra|first=Anthony W.|last=Knapp|series=Cornerstones|publisher=Springer|year=2007|isbn=9780817645229|page=446|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=25JfJAgqC8sC&pg=PA446}}.</ref> Let <math>J</math> and <math>K</math> be ideals of a commutative ring <math>R</math>, with neither one contained in the other. Then there exist <math> a\in J \setminus K</math> and <math> b\in K \setminus J</math>, where neither is in <math> J \cap K</math> but the product is. This proves that a reducible ideal is not prime. A concrete example of this are the ideals <math>2 \mathbb Z</math> and <math>3 \mathbb Z</math> contained in <math>\mathbb Z</math>. The intersection is <math>6 \mathbb Z</math>, and <math>6 \mathbb Z</math> is not a prime ideal.
* Every irreducible ideal of a [[Noetherian ring]] is a [[primary ideal]],<ref name="m98"/> and consequently for Noetherian rings an irreducible decomposition is a [[primary decomposition]].<ref name="Dummit">{{cite book|last1=Dummit|first1=David S.|last2=Foote|first2=Richard M.|title=Abstract Algebra|date=2004|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Inc.|location=Hoboken, NJ|isbn=0-471-43334-9|pages=683–685|edition=Third}}</ref>
* Every primary ideal of a [[principal ideal domain]] is an irreducible ideal. 
* Every irreducible ideal is [[primal ideal|primal]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Fuchs | first = Ladislas
 | doi = 10.2307/2032421
 | journal = [[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]]
 | mr = 0032584
 | pages = 1–6
 | title = On primal ideals
 | volume = 1
 | year = 1950| issue = 1
 | jstor = 2032421
 | doi-access = free
 }}. Theorem 1, p.&nbsp;3.</ref>
*Every irreducible ideal that is also radical is prime.  The ideal <math>4\mathbb{Z}</math> is an example of an irreducible ideal in <chem>\mathbb{Z}</chem> that is not radical and not a prime ideal.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Prime ideals and irreducible ideals |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/100837/prime-ideals-and-irreducible-ideals |access-date=2025-12-17 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange |language=en}}</ref>

==Properties ==

An element of an [[integral domain]] is [[prime element|prime]] [[if and only if]] the ideal [[principal ideal|generated by it]] is a non-zero prime ideal. This is not true for irreducible ideals; an irreducible ideal may be generated by an element that is not an [[irreducible element]], as is the case in <math>\mathbb Z</math> for the ideal <math>4 \mathbb Z</math> since it is not the intersection of two strictly greater ideals.

In [[algebraic geometry]], if an ideal <math>I</math> of a ring <math>R</math> is irreducible, then <math>V(I)</math> is an [[irreducible space|irreducible]] subset in the [[Zariski topology]] on the [[spectrum of a ring|spectrum]] <math>\operatorname{Spec} R</math>. The [[converse (logic)|converse]] does not hold; for example the ideal <math>(x^2,xy,y^2)</math> in <math>\mathbb C[x,y]</math> defines the irreducible [[algebraic variety|variety]] consisting of just the origin, but it is not an irreducible ideal as <math>(x^2,xy,y^2) = (x^2,y) \cap (x,y^2) </math>.
